newsitem.title: UK: Nickel hits nine-month high, steeled for more gain.
newsitem.headline: Nickel hits nine-month high, steeled for more gain.

text.p: Nickel prices briefly reached fresh nine-month highs again on Tuesday on the London Metal Exchange (LME) and remain in good shape to push higher despite a slight slip, analysts said.
Three months metal hit an early peak of $8,120 a tonne, then eased to end the morning session at $8,070, a $15 decline from Monday, but still up some $300 from a week ago.
"It has come back a bit today - partly in reaction to Monday's gains, but also because the copper market is looking a bit soggy," one trader said.

Latest gains were sparked by a moderate 66-tonne fall in LME warehouse stocks but the extent of the price rise over the last week, although not untypical for nickel, suggests a breather is needed, technical traders said.
In the very short-term the market may settle back towards $8,000 once more before heading towards targets near $8,450 and $8,500.

Nickel has also been boosted this week by concerns over possible supply disruptions from Russia's troubled Norilsk Nickel plant. On Monday, workers at Norilsk's main plant decided to hold a meeting on March 1 to discuss the possibility of taking action that could disrupt output.
Rumblings of discontent at Norilsk recently have centred on non-payment of salaries, although traders doubt whether workers would be prepared to take prolonged strike action.
In 1996, Norilsk Nickel produced 100,000 tonnes of nickel and it projects flat 1997 production. The combine accounts for over 50 percent of the group's total output.

General fundamental impetus for nickel price strength emanates from a strong stainless-steel sector while major non-ferrous metal companies are reporting strong incoming orders and optimism for this year.
At present, the market appears to be in equilibrium with only a modest increase in supply likely this year, UBS Ltd said in an outlook.
"We continue to expect a rebound in demand for stainless steel, which absorbs about two-thirds of all nickel consumed," UBS said.

But it is not only stainless steel that drives the nickel market. The metal is also used in high-performance alloys in the aircraft industry, LME trader Billiton Metals Ltd said in its latest weekly report.

A combination of improved airline profitability, rising demand and new noise regulations in North America and Western Europe will underscore aircraft production through to the end of the decade, Billiton noted. --London Newsroom 44 171 542 8080
